glossary.Endocardial surface: The smooth inner lining of the heart chambers and valves.
glossary.Transient bacteraemia: Bacteria in the blood for a short time, for example after dental work.
glossary.Embolisation: A fragment breaking off and lodging in a blood vessel downstream.
glossary.IV drug injection: Injecting drugs into a vein, which can introduce skin bacteria into the blood.
glossary.GI/GU surgery: Operations on the gut (gastrointestinal) or urinary and genital (genitourinary) tract.
glossary.Prosthetic valves: Artificial heart valves, mechanical or tissue.
glossary.Congenital heart disease: Heart structural abnormalities present from birth.
glossary.Tricuspid valve: Valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.
glossary.Mitral valve: Valve between the left atrium and left ventricle.
glossary.Night sweats: Heavy sweating at night, a classic sign of infection or cancer.
glossary.Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell.
glossary.Murmur: Sound of turbulent blood flow through the heart, heard with a stethoscope.
glossary.Acute mesenteric ischaemia: Sudden loss of blood supply to the gut, here from an embolus.
glossary.Strep. sanguinis: A viridans-group streptococcus from the mouth, linked to dental disease.
glossary.Alpha-haemolytic: Bacteria that partly break down red cells on blood agar, giving a green colour.
glossary.Beta-haemolytic: Bacteria that completely break down red cells on blood agar, giving a clear zone.
glossary.Gamma-haemolytic: Bacteria that do not break down red cells on blood agar.
glossary.Strep. gallolyticus: The newer name for Strep. bovis, linked to colorectal cancer.
glossary.Colorectal carcinoma: Cancer of the colon or rectum.
glossary.Gram-negative: Bacteria with a thin cell wall that stain pink on Gram staining.
glossary.Fastidious: Hard to grow in the lab because it needs special conditions.
glossary.Indwelling lines: Catheters left in a vein for a long time.
glossary.Blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to grow and identify bacteria.
glossary.Vascular phenomena: Duke minor criteria from emboli, such as Janeway lesions or infarcts.
glossary.Immunological phenomena: Duke minor criteria from immune complexes, such as Osler's nodes or Roth spots.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.Colonoscopy: Camera examination of the large bowel.
glossary.Posterior lesions: Abnormalities at the back of the heart, better seen from the oesophagus on TOE.
glossary.ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: structured assessment of an unwell patient.
glossary.Empirical: Started before the organism is known, covering the likely causes.
glossary.Ceftriaxone: A broad-spectrum cephalosporin antibiotic given IV.
glossary.Synergy: Two drugs working better together than the sum of each alone.
glossary.Haemodynamic instability: Blood pressure and pulse not maintaining adequate circulation.
glossary.MR: Mitral regurgitation: a leaky mitral valve.
glossary.Paravalvular abscess: A pocket of pus in the tissue around a heart valve.
glossary.Cardiothoracic surgery: Surgery on the heart and chest.
glossary.Antibiotic prophylaxis: Antibiotics given before a procedure to prevent infection.
glossary.Mechanical valve: A metal artificial heart valve needing lifelong warfarin.
glossary.Platelet-fibrin thrombus: A small clot of platelets and fibrin that forms on damaged endocardium.
glossary.Turbulent flow: Disorganised blood flow that damages the valve lining.
glossary.Annulus: The fibrous ring that supports a heart valve.
glossary.AV node: Atrioventricular node, which passes electrical signals from atria to ventricles.
glossary.Conduction disease: Damage to the heart's electrical pathways, causing heart block.
glossary.Venous return: Blood flowing back to the right heart through the veins.
glossary.Right heart: The right atrium and ventricle, which pump blood to the lungs.
glossary.Fungal: Caused by a fungus, such as Candida.
